levelIntroduction.title: Welcome to Logic Lab! 🧩
levelIntroduction.description: Logic puzzles are like solving mysteries! You need to think step-by-step and figure out what makes sense. In code, logic helps us solve problems by thinking carefully about each piece.

concepts.name: What is Logic?
concepts.explanation: Logic is about thinking through problems step by step. Each step needs to make sense and lead to the solution!

concepts.name: Variables and Values
concepts.explanation: Variables are like boxes that hold information. We need to be careful when moving things between boxes so we don't lose anything!

concepts.name: Order Matters
concepts.explanation: The order we do things in code is very important. Doing steps in the wrong order can cause problems!

levelIntroduction.readyMessage: Ready to solve some spooky logic puzzles? Let's go!

challenges.title: The Swapped Variables
challenges.description: The ghost wants to swap two treasure chests so chest1 has 'silver' and chest2 has 'gold'. Fix the code so it outputs: silver gold
challenges.tip: To swap two variables, you need a temporary variable to hold one value while you move things around!
hints: When chest1 = chest2 runs, the 'gold' value is lost forever!
You need to save the 'gold' value somewhere safe before overwriting chest1.
Try: save chest1 to a temp variable, then assign chest2 to chest1, then assign temp to chest2.
challenges.educationalContent: To swap two variables, we need a temporary variable to hold one value while we move things around. It's like swapping drinks between two cups - you need a third cup to hold one drink temporarily!

challenges.title: The Wrong Order
challenges.description: The ghost is trying to use a variable before it exists! Fix the code so it outputs: Total: 15
challenges.tip: Variables must be declared (created) before you can use them. Code runs from top to bottom!
hints: You can't use a variable before you create it!
The variable 'total' is used before it's created.
Move the 'let total' line before the console.log!
challenges.educationalContent: Variables must be declared (created) before you can use them. The computer reads code from top to bottom, so make sure you create variables before trying to use them!

challenges.title: The Calculation Error
challenges.description: The ghost is calculating the area of a rectangle, but the formula is wrong! Fix it so it outputs: Area: 15
challenges.tip: Area of a rectangle is width × height. Use * to multiply in code!
hints: Area of a rectangle is width times height, not width plus height!
The '+' operator adds numbers, but we need to multiply.
Change '+' to '*' to multiply width and height!
challenges.educationalContent: Math operators in code work like in math class: '+' adds, '-' subtracts, '*' multiplies, and '/' divides. Make sure you use the right operator for what you're calculating!

challenges.title: The String Number Confusion
challenges.description: The ghost is trying to add numbers, but they're being treated as text! Fix it so it outputs: Total: 30
challenges.tip: Numbers in quotes are text! Convert strings to numbers using Number() or parseInt() to do math.
hints: When you add strings with '+', they stick together instead of adding mathematically!
Convert the strings to numbers first using Number() or parseInt()!
challenges.educationalContent: In JavaScript, numbers in quotes like '10' are treated as text (strings), not numbers. When you add strings, they stick together (concatenate). To do math, convert strings to numbers using Number() or parseInt()!

challenges.title: The Array Index Mystery
challenges.description: The ghost wants to get the first ghost from the list. Fix it so it outputs: First ghost: Casper
challenges.tip: Arrays start counting at 0! The first item is at index 0, not 1.
hints: Arrays in programming start counting at 0, not 1!
ghosts[1] gives you the SECOND item, not the first.
Change the index to 0 to get the first item: ghosts[0]!
challenges.educationalContent: Arrays (lists) in programming start counting at 0! So the first item is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on. This is called 'zero-based indexing' and it's used in most programming languages!
